pairs.question: Quo titulo, a vidulo ducto, Plautus fabulam suam quae hodie fragmentis tantum superest inscripsit?
pairs.question_en: By what title, taken from a vidulus (trunk), did Plautus name his play that survives today only in fragments?
pairs.derivation: The prologue names the play ('poeta hanc noster fecit Vidulariam'); the title derives from the vidulus (traveling-trunk) central to the surviving fragments. Anchored to Plautus + the play; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ibi ut piscabar, fuscina ici vidulum.
pairs.question: Quo instrumento piscator, dum piscatur, vidulum in mari repperit apud Plautum in Vidularia?
pairs.question_en: With what implement did the fisherman, while fishing, come upon the trunk in the sea in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.derivation: A surviving fragment: while fishing, the fisherman struck the vidulus (trunk) with his fuscina (trident/fish-spear). Fishing realia; anchored to the play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: vidulum hic apponite; ego servabo, quasi sequestro detis; neutri reddibo, donicum res iudicata erit haec.
pairs.question: Quo iure Gorgines vidulum de quo lis erat apud se servat, neutri redditurus donec res iudicetur, apud Plautum in Vidularia?
pairs.question_en: In what capacity does Gorgines keep the disputed trunk, to be given back to neither party until the case is decided, in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.derivation: Legal realia: disputed property is deposited with a sequester, a neutral holder who returns it to neither party until judgment. Anchored to Gorgines + the play; short answer supported verbatim (quasi sequestro).

pairs.source_text: si tibi pudico homine est opus et non malo, qui fidei plenior sit quam servi tui, minime mendace, em me licet conducere.
pairs.question: Quid Nicodemus adulescens, inopia coactus, seni Diniae apud Plautum in Vidularia se facere offert?
pairs.question_en: What does the young Nicodemus, driven by poverty, offer to the old man Dinia in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.answer_en: To hire himself out as a laborer.
pairs.derivation: A clear scene: the impoverished freeborn youth Nicodemus offers to hire himself out to Dinia as a laborer (mercennarius). Realia of free poverty and hired labor; anchored to Nicodemus + Dinia + play; short answer supported by source (em me licet conducere).

pairs.source_text: nec mihi nisi unum prandium quicquam duis, praeter mercedem. Quid merendam? Ne duis, neque cenam.
pairs.question: Praeter mercedem et unum prandium, quas cibi vices Nicodemus operarius sibi dari opus esse negat apud Plautum in Vidularia?
pairs.question_en: Besides his wage and a single lunch, which meals does the laborer Nicodemus say he need not be given in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.derivation: Realia of the Roman meal-day: prandium (midday meal), merenda (afternoon snack), cena (dinner). Nicodemus asks only for one prandium, refusing merenda and cena. Anchored to the play; two-item answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vbi habitas? Hic apud piscatorem Gorginem.
pairs.question: Apud quem piscatorem Nicodemus adulescens habitat apud Plautum in Vidularia?
pairs.question_en: With which fisherman does the young Nicodemus lodge in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.derivation: A clear fragment: Nicodemus lodges with the fisherman Gorgines, who proves to be Dinia's neighbor. Anchored to the named characters + play; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: immo etiam argenti minam, quam med oravisti ut darem tibi faenore, iam ego adferam ad te. faenus mihi nullum duis.
pairs.question: Quantam pecuniam Dinia senex Nicodemo egenti sine ullo faenore mutuam dare pollicetur apud Plautum in Vidularia?
pairs.question_en: How much money does the old man Dinia promise to lend the needy Nicodemus without any interest in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.derivation: Money-lending realia: Dinia lends a mina of silver, waiving the interest (faenus) Nicodemus had offered. Anchored to Dinia + Nicodemus + play; short answer supported verbatim (argenti minam... faenus nullum).

pairs.source_text: Eiusdem Bacchae fecerunt nostram navem Pentheum.
pairs.question: Cuius regis exitui, a Bacchis discerpti, navem suam tempestate laceratam quidam apud Plautum in Vidularia comparat?
pairs.question_en: To the fate of which king, torn apart by the Bacchae, does a character in Plautus' Vidularia compare his storm-shattered ship?
pairs.derivation: Myth as shared story: Pentheus torn to pieces by the Bacchae; a surviving fragment says the same Bacchae 'made our ship a Pentheus.' Anchored to the play; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.question: Cuius deae sacra est myrtus, ut apud Plautum in Vidularia dicitur?
pairs.question_en: To which goddess is the myrtle sacred, as stated in Plautus' Vidularia?
pairs.derivation: Cult and plant lore: the myrtle is the plant sacred to Venus. A surviving fragment states 'haec myrtus Veneris est.' Anchored to the play; one-name answer verbatim.
